Family Health

Breast tenderness: ten possible causes and ways to find relief

Updated: October 6, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Breast tenderness can feel like soreness when touched, fullness, aching, burning or throbbing. It may affect one breast or both, come and go with periods, or start after a change in feeding, activity or medication. Many causes are benign, but persistent pain and new breast changes deserve attention. Understanding the pattern can help you decide what to try and what to discuss with a clinician.

Start with the pattern and any new changes

Breast pain can happen to anyone with breast tissue. Sometimes the discomfort begins in the breast itself; sometimes a muscle, rib or nearby joint is responsible. The location alone cannot reliably tell you which tissue is causing the pain.

Notice when the discomfort began, whether it is on one or both sides, whether movement or pressure triggers it, and whether it changes with your menstrual cycle. A short symptom diary can be useful, particularly if pain repeatedly appears before a period.

Breast pain on its own is rarely a sign of cancer. That reassurance does not mean a new lump, nipple change or persistent focal pain should be ignored. There is also no need to endure severe pain simply because a cause is likely to be benign. The ten groups below explain common possibilities and the limits of home care.

1. A bra that presses, rubs or does not support you

A bra can contribute to tenderness when its band, straps, seams or cups press into sensitive tissue. Insufficient support may also allow uncomfortable movement during walking or exercise. Breast size and preferred support can change with pregnancy, breastfeeding, weight changes and the menstrual cycle.

Check whether the cups cut into breast tissue or gape, the band rides up, straps dig in, or a wire sits on the breast rather than around it. Spilling over a cup or repeatedly adjusting the bra can be a clue that its shape or size is unsuitable. The hook you use, by itself, does not diagnose a poor fit.

Try a comfortable supportive fit and reassess during movement, not only while standing still. A fitting service can help, but it is optional. A soft bra at night may be more comfortable for some people; others prefer none. Avoid a garment that squeezes a tender area.

2. Strain in the chest muscles

The pectoral muscles lie behind the breasts. Straining them during weights, sport, shovelling, lifting bags or repeatedly carrying a child may produce pain that seems to come from the breast. It can be more noticeable on one side and worsen with certain arm or shoulder movements. A more substantial injury may cause bruising, swelling or restricted movement.

Temporarily reduce the activity that provokes the pain and return gradually as symptoms improve. Gentle movement within a comfortable range is preferable to forcing a stretch. Yoga or Pilates is not automatically suitable for a fresh injury; avoid any movement that reproduces pain.

A wrapped cold pack after an injury or gentle warmth for muscle tightness may help comfort. Ask about suitable pain relief if you need it. Seek assessment for severe pain, significant swelling, weakness or symptoms that are not improving. New chest pressure with breathlessness, sweating or faintness needs emergency care rather than an assumption that you have pulled a muscle.

3. A knock, pressure or other minor injury

Breast tissue can become sore after a bump, a heavy bag strap, pressure while carrying a child, or uncomfortable contact during sex. A minor injury may leave a tender or bruised area for several days, although recovery depends on its severity.

Reduce pressure on the area and choose clothing or a bra that feels comfortable. A cold pack wrapped in fabric can soothe recent bruising; avoid placing ice directly on skin. Pain relief may be appropriate if it is safe for you.

Do not assume that every lump after an injury is simply a bruise. Arrange an examination if a lump persists, swelling increases, the skin changes, or the pain is more severe than expected. Discuss comfortable positioning and touch with a partner rather than continuing contact that hurts.

4. Hormonal changes around a period

Changing estrogen and progesterone levels can make breast tissue feel fuller, heavier or more sensitive during the menstrual cycle. Cyclical pain often affects both breasts, especially the outer areas, and may extend towards the armpits or arms. It commonly worsens before a period and settles as the period begins or ends.

A supportive bra, a comfortable warm or cool compress, and appropriate pain relief may help. Sleep, rest and relaxation can make persistent discomfort easier to manage; this does not mean the pain is imagined or caused by a failure to relax.

Some people notice improvement when they reduce caffeine, but research has not established a consistent benefit. Avoid presenting caffeine restriction or a low-salt diet as a dependable treatment for breast pain. A balanced diet is reasonable without removing multiple foods in search of a cure.

If a recurring pattern disrupts daily life, discuss it with a clinician. Hormonal contraception may improve symptoms for some people and cause or worsen tenderness in others. The choice depends on your symptoms, medical history and contraceptive needs.

5. Pregnancy-related tenderness

Breasts may become fuller and more sensitive early in pregnancy as hormones change. Nipple sensitivity may also increase. Other possible early symptoms include a missed period, tiredness, nausea with or without vomiting, more frequent urination, constipation, heartburn or changes in taste. These symptoms vary and do not confirm pregnancy.

If pregnancy is possible, use a pregnancy test at the appropriate time and seek advice if the result or timing is unclear. Breast tenderness alone cannot tell you whether you are pregnant or whether a pregnancy is progressing normally.

A bra with room for changing breast size, soft clothing and reduced friction may help. Soft nipple pads can be useful if fabric rubbing is uncomfortable; keep them clean and change them if damp. An optional soft sleep bra or a gently warm cloth may improve comfort, but avoid heat that burns or increases swelling.

New lumps, one-sided redness, fever or unusual discharge still need assessment during pregnancy. Check any medicine with a pharmacist or maternity professional rather than applying ordinary over-the-counter pain advice without considering pregnancy.

6. Breastfeeding, attachment and nipple problems

Pain during feeding may relate to shallow attachment, friction, damaged nipple skin, uncomfortable pump fit or breast fullness. Nipples that crack, bleed, become flattened after feeds or hurt throughout each feed are reasons to ask for help early. A breastfeeding specialist can watch a feed and assess both positioning and milk transfer.

When a breast is very full, expressing a small amount may soften the area around the nipple enough to help attachment. If direct feeding is too painful, get help with an appropriate expression plan that meets the baby’s needs. Pumping more and more to completely empty the breast can increase supply and aggravate inflammation.

Tender lumpy areas are sometimes described as blocked ducts. Avoid trying to force a lump out with deep massage or strong pressure. Cold packs and gentle handling are usually more suitable for inflammation; repeated intense heat can worsen swelling.

Change damp breast pads and protect sore skin from friction. Some guidance suggests applying a little expressed milk to cracked nipples, but this is not a substitute for correcting attachment or assessing a wound that is not healing. There is no need to buy a particular pad material as a treatment.

Itching, burning or shooting pain needs an assessment rather than an automatic diagnosis of thrush. Nipple skin infection, dermatitis, trauma and blood-vessel spasm can overlap in appearance. If a clinician suspects a fungal infection, they can assess the baby too and advise treatment. Deep breast pain alone does not establish Candida infection.

When returning to work, plan feeding or expression around the baby’s usual needs and your comfort. A practical routine and well-fitting pump equipment can help avoid both uncomfortable fullness and unnecessary extra stimulation.

7. Contraception, fertility treatment and other hormonal medicines

Hormonal contraception, fertility medicines and menopausal hormone therapy can cause breast tenderness. Some contraceptive pills contain estrogen and a progestogen; others contain only a progestogen. Their effects vary. Headaches, bleeding changes or mood symptoms may occur with some products, but every user does not experience every possible side effect.

Tell the prescriber when the pain began and whether it followed a new medicine or dose change. They may suggest waiting for an initial adjustment period, changing the formulation or considering another method. A hormonal intrauterine device does not guarantee freedom from breast tenderness.

If contraception is needed, options such as condoms or a copper intrauterine device can be discussed without leaving a gap in pregnancy prevention. Do not stop an essential medicine or fertility treatment without a plan.

For menopausal treatment, a change in dose or route may be considered individually. Systemic hormone tablets, patches or gels and local vaginal estrogen preparations have different purposes and are not simply interchangeable. Persistent or new breast changes still require assessment even when a medicine seems a plausible explanation.

8. Fibrocystic breast changes

Fibrocystic changes describe tissue that can feel lumpy, thickened or rope-like, sometimes with small cysts. They are common and are not themselves the same as cancer. Some people have no discomfort; others notice tenderness or fullness, particularly in the upper outer breasts.

Symptoms often become more noticeable before a period and ease afterwards. The pattern and degree of lumpiness vary between people and across cycles.

Comfortable support, a warm or cool compress and suitable pain relief can help. If symptoms remain troublesome, discuss further options with a clinician. A new or persistent lump, a previously assessed lump that enlarges, or a breast change that remains after your period should be checked instead of being labelled fibrocystic at home.

9. Mastitis and breast infection

Mastitis involves breast inflammation and may develop into a bacterial infection. It often begins quickly in one breast, with a painful hot area, swelling or a firm region. Redness may be less obvious on darker skin. Fever, chills, aching or feeling generally unwell can accompany the local symptoms.

During lactation, continue ordinary responsive feeding if possible, rest and use gentle measures for comfort. Avoid tight pressure, deep massage and expressing extra milk in an effort to clear the breast. A cold compress can help. A feeding specialist can assist if the baby cannot attach or feeding is too painful.

Antibiotics are appropriate for bacterial mastitis when clinically indicated; inflammation does not automatically require them. Contact a clinician if symptoms are worsening or have not started improving after twelve to twenty-four hours of home measures. If prescribed antibiotics are not helping within forty-eight hours, seek reassessment. Do not wait for these time points if you feel severely ill.

A persistent painful lump or worsening illness can indicate an abscess, which may need imaging and drainage. Mastitis can also occur in people who are not breastfeeding, including men, and should be assessed. Treatment and recovery times depend on the cause; there is no guaranteed one-week course or universal recovery deadline.

10. A breast cyst

A cyst is a pocket of fluid within breast tissue. It may feel round or oval, soft or quite firm, and there may be one or several in either breast. Some are painless; others become tender or more noticeable before a period and smaller afterwards. Touch alone cannot reliably distinguish a cyst from a solid lump.

A clinician may examine the breast and arrange ultrasound or other investigations according to your age, history and findings. New nipple discharge should be assessed rather than assumed to come from a harmless cyst.

A confirmed simple cyst that causes no symptoms may need no treatment. A large or painful cyst can sometimes be drained with a fine needle. Persistent lumps, bloody fluid or a lump that does not disappear after drainage may require further investigation. Cysts can recur.

A comfortable bra, a compress and suitable pain relief may ease tenderness. Cutting salt is not an established way to remove cysts, and diet changes do not replace assessment of a new lump.

Use pain relief that fits your circumstances

Paracetamol, also called acetaminophen, or an anti-inflammatory such as ibuprofen may be suitable for some causes of breast pain. Naproxen is another anti-inflammatory, but these medicines are not appropriate for everyone. Ask about interactions and conditions such as kidney disease, stomach ulcers or previous reactions to anti-inflammatory medicines.

Follow the product instructions and avoid combining medicines with the same active ingredient. If a topical pain gel is recommended, check where it can be applied and how to prevent contact with a feeding baby; do not put it on damaged nipples without specific advice.

During pregnancy, do not self-treat with ibuprofen, naproxen or other NSAIDs. They should be avoided from twenty weeks unless a clinician specifically advises otherwise. Prescribed low-dose aspirin has a separate role and should not be stopped on the basis of general pain-medicine advice. Breastfeeding also warrants a product-specific check.

When to get help and what an assessment can involve

Seek prompt medical care for a new lump, skin dimpling or an orange-peel appearance, a change in breast shape, a newly inverted nipple, a persistent nipple rash or unusual discharge, especially blood. A hot swollen breast with fever or chills also needs timely advice. You do not need to have several warning signs together.

Call emergency services for severe chest pain with breathing difficulty, collapse, confusion or other signs of a serious acute illness. These symptoms should not be attributed to ordinary breast tenderness.

For persistent pain without emergency symptoms, book an appointment if it is worsening, interfering with sleep or activities, or not responding to simple measures. Mention pregnancy or feeding, medicines, prior breast problems and family history. Assessment may involve an examination and, when appropriate, imaging or referral.

Finding the cause can take more than one visit. Bring your symptom pattern and questions, and return if a previously assessed problem changes. Relief may be gradual, and the aim is a clear explanation and a workable plan rather than a promise that every cause will resolve within one or two weeks.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Breast-health guidance distinguishes cyclical pain, pain arising outside the breast and symptoms requiring investigation. A symptom pattern can guide assessment, but a new lump or nipple change should be evaluated even when tenderness appears hormonal.

Lactation advice has changed: excessive pumping and deep massage may aggravate inflammation, and not all mastitis is bacterial. Breastfeeding pain should be assessed before diagnosing thrush. Pregnancy changes the suitability of pain medicines.

How BeMama can help

Record the pattern of pain and any new changes, then choose comfort measures and professional support that fit your situation.

When to seek help

Seek timely care for new breast or nipple changes, a hot swollen breast or fever. Severe chest pain with breathing difficulty, collapse or confusion requires emergency help.

Evidence notes updated: October 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Breast tenderness has several possible causes, and the pattern is useful information.
  • A comfortable bra and cause-appropriate self-care may help, but new lumps or nipple changes need assessment.
  • Get early feeding support for persistent nipple pain; avoid deep breast massage and extra pumping.
  • Check medicines during pregnancy or breastfeeding rather than using a general pain recommendation.

Frequently asked questions

Does breast pain mean breast cancer?

Pain alone is rarely a cancer symptom. A new lump, persistent focal pain, skin change, nipple inversion or unusual discharge still needs assessment. A reassuring pattern does not replace checking a new change.

Why do both breasts hurt before my period?

Hormonal changes can make both breasts fuller and more sensitive before a period. Tracking the pattern may help. Seek advice if symptoms are severe, persistent or accompanied by a new breast change.

Can a bra make my breasts sore?

Pressure, friction or inadequate support can contribute. Check the cups, band and straps during movement. A comfortable supportive fit may help; wearing a soft bra at night is a personal comfort choice.

How can I tell whether pain comes from a muscle?

Pain that changes with arm movement or follows lifting may come from the chest wall, but the pattern cannot confirm this. Severe, unexplained or persistent pain needs assessment. Chest pressure with breathlessness or faintness needs emergency care.

Does tenderness prove that I am pregnant?

No. Period-related changes, medicines and other causes can feel similar. If pregnancy is possible, take a pregnancy test at the appropriate time rather than relying on breast symptoms.

Should I massage a painful breast lump while breastfeeding?

Avoid deep massage or firm pressure. Inflammation can worsen with forceful handling or extra pumping. Seek feeding support, and arrange assessment for a persistent lump, fever or worsening symptoms.

Is shooting breast pain always thrush?

No. Attachment problems, trauma, skin conditions and blood-vessel spasm can cause similar pain. A clinician should assess the symptoms and the baby when relevant before recommending antifungal treatment.

Should I stop my contraceptive pill or hormone treatment?

Discuss a possible medicine-related cause with the prescriber. An alternative may help, but do not stop essential treatment or leave a gap in contraception without a plan.

Do breast cysts need to be drained?

Not always. A confirmed simple cyst without symptoms may be left alone. A large or painful cyst may benefit from aspiration. New, persistent or changing lumps require assessment before being treated as cysts.

Will cutting caffeine or salt cure breast pain?

There is limited evidence for dietary changes as treatment. Some people find less caffeine helpful, but it is not a guaranteed cure, and salt restriction has not been established as a cyst or breast-pain treatment.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
